title: The Hours
full_review:
"The Hours" (Paramount) looks at a traumatic day in the lives of three women in different decades -- British author Virginia Woolf, a Los Angeles housewife and a New York City editor.

Based on Michael Cunningham's novel, it deals with the characters' sexual orientations and desires to end their lives, making it not a movie to see for casual entertainment. In fact, the film opens with Woolf's suicide by drowning in 1941 and closes on it as well.

Director Stephen Daldry gets evocative performances from his three female leads and is skillful in weaving the three stories together by the slender thread of "Mrs. Dalloway," the novel Virginia Woolf (an unrecognizable Nicole Kidman) is struggling to write on the day we see her in 1923.

The film jumps ahead to 1951 Los Angeles where severely depressed homemaker Laura (Julianne Moore) is reading the novel, and to 2001 where gay editor Clarissa (Meryl Streep) is planning a party for her AIDS-stricken poet friend, Rich (Ed Harris). The one-day aspect parallels the novel's story of one day in the life of its title character, Clarissa Dalloway.

We see that Virginia is as much troubled by her debilitating mental illness, which includes hearing voices, as she is by her devoted husband's (Stephen Dillane) hovering attentions. A visit from her sister (Miranda Richardson), whom she kisses on the lips, is but a brief distraction from her internal demons.

Pregnant Laura is struggling to make a birthday cake with her little son Rich (Jack Rovello) for her loving but clueless husband (John C. Reilly). After comforting a sick friend (Toni Colette) with words and a direct kiss, she is tortured by suicidal thoughts so leaves the preschooler with a sitter and heads for a hotel room.

Lesbian editor Clarissa visits the now middle-aged Rich, who is in the final stages of AIDS and seems none too willing to attend a poetry awards ceremony in his honor and her party afterward.

As the film crosscuts among the three locales and eras we learn how Virginia is resentful that doctors and her husband are in charge of her care when she feels she alone should decide what is best for her. She also feels his life and career are diminished by her psychiatric condition.

Laura has been hiding depression for years, surely linked to sexual orientation issues.

Clarissa does not want to face the fact that Rich is dying. He thanks her for keeping him alive by nursing him for 10 years but now he wants her to let him go and focus on her own life. Calling her his nickname for her -- Mrs. Dalloway -- he recites tender words from the novel and goes out the tenement window to his death.

In the final scene, Laura, Rich's long-estranged and elderly mom, visits Clarissa the night of his death and talks of the day she nearly committed suicide. She reveals that she could not kill her unborn baby and chose life instead -- but abandoned her family after her daughter was born.

Clarissa retires to her bedroom where her lover (Allison Janney) offers her a sympathetic ear and Clarissa responds with an emphatic kiss.

The beautifully acted picture is most problematic in its sympathetic depiction of suicide and the active gay lifestyle. However, it is poignant in its focus on the frail and fractured humanity of the wounded souls on display as the characters struggle to do what is right or what they perceive is right for themselves and their loved ones.

Nonetheless, characters make wrongheaded choices, such as committing suicide partly to relieve others of the daily burden of their care. This nonjudgmental view of suicide as acceptable or just another choice runs contrary to Catholic teaching.

Virginia and Rich seem to justify killing themselves by seeing it as a gift of life to the person they leave behind. On the other hand, suicidal Laura made a life-affirming choice which saved her baby's life and her own, though we know little about her life after she left her family. The active gay lifestyle is presented in Clarissa's case as a contemporary reality that, despite its sobering potential for contracting a fatal illness, allows Clarissa to be comforted and find peace.

Homosexual desire is a source of anguish for Laura and much more subtly for Virginia. (For those unfamiliar with Woolf's life and writings, her story -- as filmed -- suggests mental illness, not repressed sexuality, as the core of her problem.) Many viewers are likely to be disturbed by the prolonged same-sex kisses, Clarissa's openly gay lifestyle and her casual remark that she had a daughter by someone she never met (apparently by artificial insemination).

A sensitive and multilayered story, "The Hours" is a thoughtful and disturbing contemplation about people in crisis, but the film's indulgent attitude toward the choices they make poses a moral problem for viewers.

Because of a sympathetic treatment of suicide, several instances of same-sex kissing, minimal profanity and an instance of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
